name: Scythians and Saka
summary: Iranian-speaking nomadic horse peoples of the Eurasian steppe, from the Black Sea (Scythians) to Central Asia (Saka). They were famed horse archers, and their gold work and burial mounds survive.

knownFor.label: Scythian gold
knownFor.note: Animal-style gold work such as the Tolstaya Mogila pectoral.

knownFor.label: Horse archers
knownFor.note: Riders who shot short composite bows from the saddle.

knownFor.label: Kurgans
knownFor.note: Large burial mounds for chiefs, with horses and treasures.

location.value: The steppes from the northern Black Sea coast to the Altai and Central Asia.

terrain.value: Open grassland with river valleys; mountains in the east.

resources.value: Pasture for horses, cattle and sheep; gold from the Altai; grain from farming neighbours.

urbanisation.value: Mostly nomadic; some fortified settlements (Kamianske, Bilsk).

migration.value: Moved from Central Asia into the Black Sea steppe around the 8th–7th century BCE; Saka groups moved into Iran and India (Indo-Scythians).

economicBase.value: Herding horses, sheep and cattle; tribute and trade with farmers.

tradeRoutes.value: Traded grain, slaves and furs to Greek colonies on the Black Sea for wine, oil and fine goods.

wealth.value: Chiefs were buried with great treasures of gold.

moneyAndTax.value: No coins of their own until some Saka kings minted coins.

inequality.value: Royal clans and warriors above herders and slaves.

keyRulers.value: King Ateas (died 339 BCE). King Idanthyrsus (fought Darius I, about 513 BCE). Indo-Scythian king Maues (about 85 BCE).

succession.value: Hereditary royal clans, as described by Herodotus.

institutions.value: Councils of warriors; oaths sworn by drinking wine mixed with blood (Herodotus).

armyAndTech.value: Mounted archers with composite bows, short swords (akinakes) and scale armour.

majorWars.value: Raids into the Middle East (7th century BCE); resisted Darius I of Persia (about 513 BCE); fought Philip II of Macedon (339 BCE).

territoryChange.value: Pushed out of the western steppe by the Sarmatians (from about 200 BCE); the Crimean Scythian state lasted until about 200 CE.

alliancesRivals.value: Traded with Greeks; fought Persians and Macedonians; served as mercenaries.

inventions.value: Saddle cloths, trousers for riding, and the composite bow were used widely by steppe peoples like them.

scienceEducation.value: No writing of their own; known through Greek and Persian writers and archaeology.

openness.value: Open to trade and influence from Greeks, Persians and Chinese.

communicationTransport.value: Horses and wagons covered with felt carried whole families across the steppe.

religion.value: Worshipped gods such as Tabiti (hearth) and Papaios (sky); Herodotus describes cannabis steam rituals.

languageWriting.value: Eastern Iranian languages (related to modern Ossetian).

artsArchitecture.value: The “animal style” in gold and bronze; tattoos found on frozen mummies (Pazyryk).

socialStructure.value: Warrior aristocracy; some women were buried with weapons.

sharedIdentity.value: Shared nomadic culture across a huge area rather than one nation.

dailyLife.value: Lived in wagons and felt tents, moving between pastures; meat, mare’s milk and cheese; trousers and leather boots for riding.

neighbours.value: Greeks, Persians, Thracians, Sarmatians, Chinese states.

ideasReligions.value: Greek art influenced Scythian goldwork; steppe styles spread into Europe and China.

colonisation.value: Saka groups founded kingdoms in north-west India and Afghanistan (Indo-Scythians).

riseSignals.value: Mastery of horse riding and archery.

peakPeriod.value: Black Sea Scythians at their richest in the 4th century BCE.

declineSignals.value: Pressure from the Sarmatians and others.

outcome.value: Merged into other peoples by about the 4th century CE (Goths, Huns, Alans).

sources.value: Wikipedia: Scythians; Wikipedia: Saka; Herodotus, Histories, Book 4; Cunliffe, The Scythians (2019).

overallCertainty.value: Known mostly from Greek writers and archaeology; many details are uncertain.
